The managed path, using the Amazon SageMaker AI model package from AWS Marketplace, is the default for most teams: you subscribe, deploy to an in-VPC endpoint in minutes, and let SageMaker handle scaling and operations.

The self-managed path, running the model container yourself on EC2 GPU instances, is designed for teams with specific constraints: existing GPU infrastructure, strict networking requirements, or a need to co-locate Cartesia with other services. For these teams, full control over the runtime, scaling, and network path matters more than time to deployment.

The following table summarizes how the two compare.

CriteriaSageMaker (Marketplace)EC2 GPU (Self-Managed)
Time to DeploymentMinutes after subscribingHours to days
ComputeReal-time endpoint. See 
SupportedRealtimeInferenceInstanceTypes
for supported instances.		 EC2 GPU instances
Operational ControlManaged by AWSFull control
ScalingSageMaker automatic scalingCustom scaling policies
Cost ModelSoftware fee + per instance hour + infraEC2 (Reserved/Spot savings)
NetworkingIn-VPC endpoint (network isolation)Placement groups, Direct Connect
Best ForFast, managed, in-VPCCustom infra, max control

Beyond deploying Cartesia in your own account, these models are already proven in production inside Amazon services, and few environments are more demanding for real-time voice than a live contact center. Amazon Connect is exactly that proving ground.

In production: Amazon Connect

This section shows how Cartesia’s voice models operate inside Amazon Connect at production scale.

What is Amazon Connect?

Amazon Connect is a cloud-based contact center service that businesses use to set up and run customer support operations that handle inbound and outbound voice calls, chat, and messaging. With pay-as-you-go pricing and deep integration with AWS services, Amazon Connect powers millions of customer interactions daily across industries from financial services to healthcare.

How Cartesia powers the Amazon Connect experience

Cartesia’s voice AI models integrate natively with Amazon Connect to deliver next-generation contact center experiences:

  • Instant responsiveness: Alleviate unnatural pauses that erode customer confidence in AI-powered interactions.
  • Real-time transcription: Ink provides live transcription with intelligent turn detection for agent-assist workflows.
  • Multilingual support: Serve customers in over 44 languages with consistent voice quality and natural prosody.
  • Scalable infrastructure: Handle traffic spikes during peak hours without degradation in voice quality or latency.

By combining the omnichannel orchestration of Amazon Connect with Cartesia’s real-time voice AI, you can automate complex customer interactions while maintaining the natural, responsive experience that builds trust and loyalty.

Getting started

Ready to build ultra-low-latency voice AI applications? Here are next steps:

  • Deploy Sonic through SageMaker JumpStart: Search for “Cartesia” in the SageMaker JumpStart model hub and deploy a real-time endpoint in minutes.
  • Try the Cartesia API: Get started with the Cartesia get-started guide. No infrastructure setup required.
  • Explore reference architectures: Visit the Cartesia GitHub repository for sample notebooks, deployment templates, and integration examples.
  • Contact the team: Reach out to Cartesia on AWS Marketplace.

About the authors

entries.title: Introducing India-based inference for Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock
entries.summary: Amazon Bedrock now offers in-country inference in India for Kimi K3, keeping processing within the Mumbai and Hyderabad Regions. This post explains the global and geographic cross-Region inference options and shares example code for reading and understanding Indic-language documents with Kimi K3.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Introducing India-based inference for Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock

Kimi K3 is a multi-modal, open-weight foundation model (FM) that provider Moonshot AI reported achieved frontier-level coding and general agentic intelligence at release.

In addition to global and US-based inference, Amazon Bedrock now supports in-country inference in India for Kimi K3: unblocking local workloads with strict data residency requirements. Customers like Ultrahuman are already seeing the benefits in production:

“Jade, an AI Health and Wellness assistant in the Ultrahuman app, answers questions in plain language using each person’s own Ring and glucose data, across more than 14,000 conversations a day. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock let us add a leading open-weight model through the API we already use, with health data staying inside AWS and Mumbai as a fallback Region. With prompt caching, we’ve cut LLM costs by 80 percent and made multi-turn chats 85 percent faster.”

— Aditya Patawari, VP Engineering, Ultrahuman

In this post, we explain the different global and geographic inference options available, and share code for an example use case: optical character recognition (OCR) and understanding of Indic-language documents, with follow-up question answering in code-mixed Hinglish.

Choose where inference can run

Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock is offered through cross-Region inference profiles. You can invoke the model from any of a wide range of AWS Regions (the “source”). Amazon Bedrock then securely processes your request in one of multiple possible “destination” Regions.

Cross-Region inference is fully managed by AWS: Data is encrypted in transit between Regions and remains on the AWS network, never traversing the public internet or requiring you to set up any multi-Region virtual private cloud (VPC) infrastructure.

The inference profile ID you invoke controls which destination Regions are eligible:

ProfileModel IDWhen to choose it
Global
global.moonshotai.kimi-k3
 Recommended for most use cases: lowest cost and most broadly available
India geographic
in.moonshotai.kimi-k3
 Inference processing must stay within Mumbai and Hyderabad Regions

See the Amazon Bedrock Kimi K3 model card for up-to-date information on available inference profiles, which AWS Regions they can be called from, and what destination Regions they can use for inference.

Example walkthrough: Indic-language document understanding

Let’s consider an example use case: reading a scanned Hindi document, extracting structured data, and answering follow-up questions in mixed Hindi and English (Hinglish).

This need is common in Indian financial services and public sector workflows where know your customer (KYC) forms, utility bills, and similar documents must often be digitized. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock can directly read and reason about images, including those containing multilingual text. It offers a potential solution with no separate OCR or translation service required.

Prerequisites

The full source code for this example is available on GitHub.

To follow along, you need:

  • An AWS account.
  • Python 3.11 or later installed, with internet access to install the required PyPI packages.
  • The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed, with credentials configured with sufficient AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to invoke the Kimi K3 model through the India inference profile.

For example, to use Kimi K3 through the 

ap-south-1
Mumbai Region with India geographic inference, the following IAM policy grants sufficient access. Replace the 
{ACCOUNT_ID}
placeholders with your AWS account ID:

For more information about permissions, see Prerequisites for running model inference in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. If your organization restricts AWS Regions, ask your administrator to review the geographic cross-Region inference IAM and SCP guidance. Keep the source Region permitted and allow routing to both India destinations, using a profile-scoped exception where appropriate. The Responses API guide also describes required default-project access.

Get started with the inference APIs

As detailed on the model card, Amazon Bedrock supports multiple APIs for invoking Kimi K3, all under the Bedrock Runtime endpoint:

APIRequest and response format
Chat Completions OpenAI-compatible messages input and assistant-message output.
Responses OpenAI-compatible input and structured output items.
Converse Standardized messages, content blocks, and inference parameters across supported models.
InvokeModel Model-specific JSON request and response bodies.

Because the OpenAI-compatible APIs are recommended for this model, we use those in this example and connect through the openai Python Library.

Amazon Bedrock supports generating API keys for integrations that require them. However, AWS recommends using short-lived credentials instead where possible. The AWS token generator Python library derives a short-term API key-like token from the standard AWS CLI credential chain.

If you use a named profile for your AWS CLI, you might need to set the 

AWS_PROFILE
environment variable first. After CLI credentials are set up, you can invoke the model with the following code:

Here, 

region
(
ap-south-1
Mumbai) specifies the source Region to which the request is made. The inference profile 
in.moonshotai.kimi-k3
ensures that inference is processed in Indian Regions only.

A broad range of features like streaming, tool calling, and structured outputs are supported across both the Chat Completions and Responses APIs. See the OpenAI Python API Reference for more examples.

Analyze images

Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock supports images as well as PDFs and a range of other file types. You can send input files to the model directly by base64-encoding. For OCR or other use cases where small details are important, consider setting the image 

detail
parameter to 
high
. This improves accuracy, at the cost of more input tokens consumed per image.

In some cases, we’ve seen higher output quality for Kimi K3 when images are provided before text inputs. We suggest experimenting with request ordering. Consider the following example code:

To demonstrate, we generated an image of a synthetic electricity bill in Hindi.

Given this image input, the model can answer questions by pulling data directly from the document with no separate digitization step required. For example:

Q: Bill kitne ka hai aur last date kab hai? Late hua toh kitna dena padega?

A: Bill ka total ₹2,217.20 hai, aur last date 20/10/2026 hai. Late hua toh ₹2,261.54 dena padega.

Build a structured extraction pipeline

Beyond general question-answering, you can create structured document processing workflows by using static prompts to extract a consistent set of expected fields across many documents.

To apply firm constraints on output structure (rather than best-effort prompt-guided generation), Kimi K3 supports structured output on Amazon Bedrock either through function calling or by providing a JSON Schema output format. These options are described in more detail in the OpenAI documentation (for OpenAI-compatible APIs) and the Amazon Bedrock User Guide (for native Converse/InvokeModel APIs).

In the full sample code repository, we’ve provided an end-to-end pipeline that:

  • Transcribes the document in its original script (OCR).
  • Extracts key fields as JSON using a configurable schema, with dates normalized to ISO 8601 (
    YYYY-MM-DD
    ), Devanagari digits (for example २८८) converted to Western digits (288), and names transliterated into English.
  • Writes a short English summary.
  • Answers multi-turn follow-up questions in Hinglish (Hindi written in Latin script, mixed with English) about the same document.

For the same synthetic Hindi electricity bill in the preceding figure, the pipeline returns structured fields such as the following (abbreviated):

We’ve also included a KYC form example and an open-ended schema-free mode, where the model selects the most useful fields itself for any other document type. All provided sample documents are synthetic, with fictional names and addresses and masked identity numbers.

Download the sample code from GitHub to explore further and try it out on your own images.

As with any automated extraction, you should verify the outputs are reliable for your specific use case before relying on them for important decisions. Consider adding post-validation logic or a human review step for critical workflows.

Optimize price-performance, service tiers and caching

Tune your system prompts and schemas against example documents for reliable extractions. Amazon Bedrock Advanced Prompt Optimization (AdvPO) provides a fully managed option to optimize prompt templates based on reference examples.

Amazon Bedrock service tiers give you control over price-performance on a per-request basis. For less latency-sensitive cases, you can select the flex tier to enjoy a 50 percent discount on default standard pricing. For latency-critical scenarios, you can select “priority” to request higher queue priority at a higher price. See the pricing page for details.

Use cases with long, seldom-changing content in their input prompts can also benefit from prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock. Make sure the static content (system prompt, tool descriptions, and so on) appears at the beginning of the input, before dynamic sections like the current image and question.

Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock supports both discounted pricing for cache hits, as well as an explicit caching mode. In the default implicit caching mode, the service attempts to automatically cache and reuse repeated prompt prefixes between requests with no user action required. However, you can improve performance by selecting the explicit mode and specifying ‘breakpoints’ of cacheable content in your input, boosting cache hit rate, response speed, and cost savings.

The following example shows explicit prompt caching with the Responses API. For more information, see prompt caching in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide:

Monitor usage

Amazon CloudWatch metrics are automatically generated for Kimi K3 under the 

AWS/Bedrock
namespace, giving visibility of the invocation rate, token counts, cache usage, latency, errors, and throttling.

Model invocation logging is opt-in and can optionally contain prompts and outputs. Review access, retention, and storage location settings before enabling it.

Logs and metrics are stored in the source Region where you submitted your request, regardless of which destination Region might have processed it in cross-Region inference. You can optionally enable AWS CloudTrail data event logging to log model invocations in CloudTrail, which records requests’ destination Region as an 

additionalEventData.inferenceRegion
field.

Clean up

Kimi K3 is billed on a per-token basis, so these code samples don’t provision any persistent AWS resources to clean up. If you created a new IAM Role or User to explore with, or added extra permissions to your existing User/Role, remember to delete them when you’re finished.

Conclusion and next steps

In this post, we explored how Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock provides on-demand intelligence capable of understanding mixed Indic and English languages. It now supports fully in-country data processing in India (AWS Mumbai and Hyderabad Regions) through the 

in.moonshotai.kimi-k3
inference profile.

Try it today in the Amazon Bedrock console or through the inference APIs. Check out the model card for more information, and visit AWS re:Post to find answers or ask the community about Amazon Bedrock.

entries.title: Prepare web content for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Crawl4AI
entries.summary: This post shows how to use Crawl4AI, an open source web crawler, as a content preparation layer for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, handling JavaScript rendering, selective extraction, and custom metadata enrichment before web content reaches an Amazon S3 data source.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Prepare web content for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Crawl4AI

When you build Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) applications, answer quality depends on the data that you ingest. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the fully managed RAG capability of Amazon Bedrock. With Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, you connect your data sources, and Amazon Bedrock manages ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you. You don’t provision or scale a vector store, and embedding and reranking use service-managed models by default.

For web content, start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler data source connector for managed knowledge bases. You give it the seed URLs or sitemaps that you’re authorized to crawl, and it crawls within the scope and rate limits that you set. Scheduled syncs keep your knowledge base current as pages change, and the connector can wait for content that loads with JavaScript. There’s no crawler for you to build, host, or operate, so this connector is the starting point for most public website content.

Some sources need more control over what reaches the knowledge base. You might want to index only the main content region of each page, remove navigation and other boilerplate, or attach your own metadata attributes to every document. For that class of source material, you can extend the reach of your knowledge base with a preparation step built with Crawl4AI, an open source Python crawler. The step writes Markdown and a metadata sidecar for each page to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and the knowledge base ingests both through its Amazon S3 data source.

In this post, we show you how to choose the appropriate web ingestion path and implement custom preparation for content that needs additional processing. You then start ingestion into a managed knowledge base and validate retrieval quality. The companion aws-samples repository provides the complete workflow as a sample implementation.

This is batch ingestion of known web properties, not real-time web access at inference time such as Web Grounding with Amazon Nova.

Solution overview

Start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler when it can reach and index the pages you need. It respects 

robots.txt
, and after the first full crawl, each sync captures only added, updated, and deleted content.

Use the Crawl4AI preparation path when public source material needs one or more of the following before ingestion:

  • Structured Markdown preparation: Use 
    DefaultMarkdownGenerator
    with a pruning content filter to reduce navigation and other boilerplate while preserving headings, lists, and tables. Because pruning is heuristic, review representative output from your sites.
  • Bounded, targeted extraction: Extract only the page region that an optional CSS selector matches. Constrain breadth-first traversal by seed origin, page/path/host scope, depth and page caps, and URL patterns.
  • Custom metadata: Attach source URLs, crawl timestamps, content type, and your own attributes to each document, so that you can filter retrieval results on them.

Because managed and customer-managed knowledge bases both support Amazon S3 data sources, the Crawl4AI path works with either type. This post uses a managed knowledge base and notes where a customer-managed knowledge base differs.

The rest of this post follows the companion sample. Treat its architecture and defaults as a starting point, not as requirements of Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

By default, the sample runs the AWS Fargate task in a public subnet, where it reaches your configured websites through an internet gateway. Crawl4AI’s role ends once it has prepared the source documents and metadata sidecars. From ingestion onward, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases handles parsing, chunking, embedding, indexing, and retrieval. The following diagram shows the Crawl4AI path from the schedule through to retrieval.

The numbered steps in the diagram map to the following workflow:

  • Amazon EventBridge starts the Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task on AWS Fargate on the configured schedule.
  • The task crawls the public websites you configured and prepares Markdown with a metadata sidecar for each page.
  • The task uploads the prepared files to the Amazon S3 bucket that backs the knowledge base data source.
  • The task starts an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases ingestion job.
  • Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases reads the new and changed objects, parses them, and applies the chunking strategy you selected.
  • It creates embeddings and indexes them in the knowledge base’s vector store, which Amazon Bedrock manages for a managed knowledge base.
  • Your generative AI application queries the knowledge base for relevant chunks or for a generated response with citations.

The task reads its non-secret pipeline configuration from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store at startup.

The workflow processes public pages only and doesn’t implement authenticated sessions. For sites that require sign-in, evaluate the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler authentication options first, which include basic, form-based, and SAML authentication. Extending the sample with authentication requires session handling, credentials in AWS Secrets Manager, and a security review.

How the workflow works

The AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) app packages the implementation in a container image during deployment. When the schedule fires, the container runs 

scripts/container_entrypoint.py
and executes crawl, upload, and ingestion in sequence. The following three steps explain the core logic.

Step 1: Crawl and extract content

The crawl step performs bounded crawling and writes a Markdown file with a metadata sidecar for each successfully prepared page. The following excerpt is simplified. The module 

src/crawl4ai_bedrock_kb/crawl.py
contains the complete seed pacing, URL filtering and scoping, page limits, and redirect checks:

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports several document formats for Amazon S3 data sources, including plain text, HTML, Markdown, PDF, and DOCX. The workflow writes Markdown because it preserves headings, lists, and tables without carrying all raw HTML into ingestion.

Step 2: Upload to Amazon S3

The upload step sends each prepared Markdown document and its matching metadata sidecar to the configured S3 bucket, under the workflow’s 

s3Prefix
. For 
page.md
, the sidecar must be named 
page.md.metadata.json
, the complete source filename with 
.metadata.json
appended. The workflow stores each sidecar in the same S3 location as its document. Amazon Bedrock limits each metadata sidecar to 10 KB. If a sidecar would exceed that limit, the run stops with an error before it writes either file.

Each attribute in the sidecar uses the typed format that both managed and customer-managed knowledge bases accept for Amazon S3 data sources. The following abbreviated sidecar, formatted for readability, shows three of the attributes that the workflow writes:

The pipeline uploads only the paths produced by the current crawl, so stale local files are not sent.

Step 3: Let Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases chunk, embed, and index

After content is in S3, an ingestion job hands each document to the data source’s ingestion pipeline. By default, a managed knowledge base parses each file with its managed parser, which automatically selects a parsing approach for your content. You select the chunking strategy when you connect the data source. You can’t change it afterward, so evaluate the options before you create a production data source. A managed knowledge base offers the following chunking strategies:

  • Default chunking uses fixed-size chunks of 300 tokens with 20 percent overlap.
  • Fixed-size chunking splits content by a maximum token count and an overlap percentage that you set.
  • No chunking treats each file as a single chunk, for content that you have already split.

Chunk boundaries and retrieval results depend on the content and the selected strategy, so compare the options with representative pages and evaluation questions. To change strategies later, create a new data source. For more information, see Customize ingestion for a data source. A customer-managed knowledge base also offers semantic and hierarchical chunking and additional parsing options. For details, see How content chunking works for knowledge bases.

The workflow then starts an ingestion job so the knowledge base processes the new documents. The following simplified excerpt from 

src/crawl4ai_bedrock_kb/ingest.py
shows the call:

The same 

StartIngestionJob
and 
GetIngestionJob
calls work for both knowledge base types, and you can also monitor progress on the console.

Deploy the solution

In this section, you deploy the workflow into your AWS account with AWS CDK. Only the knowledge base prerequisites differ between the two knowledge base types. When you’re finished, follow the steps in the Clean up section to remove the resources.

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure that you have:

  • An AWS account.
  • One of the following knowledge bases:
    • A managed knowledge base, which this post uses, in an AWS Region where managed knowledge bases are available. For instructions, see Create a managed knowledge base and the Amazon S3 connector. On the data source, leave Metadata files prefix empty, because the workflow writes each metadata sidecar alongside its document.
    • An existing customer-managed knowledge base. To add an Amazon S3 data source, see Connect to Amazon S3 for your knowledge base. The workflow writes a metadata sidecar for every document, so confirm that your vector store can store and filter those attributes, as described in Metadata and filtering. For example, an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector index must use the 
      faiss
      engine. An Amazon Aurora vector index needs a custom metadata column or a column for each metadata attribute. With Amazon S3 Vectors, a capability of Amazon S3, you can attach up to 1 KB of custom metadata to each vector, so keep attributes that you add short.
  • An Amazon S3 data source in that knowledge base whose status is 
    AVAILABLE
    . It can be a new data source or one you already use. It must use the S3 bucket that you configure for this workflow. If the data source filters content by prefix or file pattern, the filters must allow the files that the workflow writes under its 
    s3Prefix
    (default 
    web-content/
    ).
  • The knowledge base, the S3 bucket, and the stack you deploy all in one Region.
  • Authorization to crawl the public websites you configure.
  • A deployment workstation with Git, Python 3.10 or later, 
    Node.js
    , the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) version 2, the AWS CDK CLI v2, and a running Docker-compatible container engine. The deployment guide lists the minimum AWS CDK CLI version.
  • AWS credentials configured on the deployment workstation with permission to bootstrap the target environment and deploy the CDK stack.
  • A bootstrapped CDK environment in the target account and Region. The deployment steps include the bootstrap command.

You need the workstation only to build and deploy. After deployment, the schedule runs the task in AWS.

Deploy the scheduled workflow

Clone the companion repository and install the deployment dependencies:

Keep Docker running. Set 

AWS_DEFAULT_REGION
to your knowledge base’s Region first, because 
cdk deploy
uses the Region from your environment or AWS profile, not the one in the bootstrap command. Bootstrap the target account and Region once, if needed. Then deploy the stack with your knowledge base, data source, S3 bucket, and authorized seed URLs:

Replace every example value, including 

ACCOUNT_ID
, 
REGION
, and the four required context keys, with your own. The example values are syntactically valid, so an unedited command deploys a stack that points at a bucket you don’t own. You can also set these keys in 
cdk.json
.

The 

maxDepth
and 
maxPages
values limit the first crawl to one link level and 25 pages. Raise them after you review the prepared output. To preview which pages a crawl prepares, you can also run the pipeline locally with 
--dry-run
, as described in the README. The stack name is fixed, so another 
cdk deploy
in the same account and Region updates this stack.

The sample builds an ARM64 container image by default. If Docker on your x86_64 workstation can’t build ARM64 images, add 

-c cpuArchitecture=X86_64
to the 
cdk deploy
command.

If your account turns on VPC Block Public Access, the task can’t reach the internet from the default public subnet. To check the mode, run 

aws ec2 describe-vpc-block-public-access-options
. In ingress-only mode, deploy with 
-c egressMode=nat
, which adds a NAT gateway with hourly charges. Bidirectional mode also needs an exclusion, as the deployment guide describes.

The stack doesn’t create or change your knowledge base or data source.

With the default 

rate(24 hours)
schedule, the first run starts when the deployment creates the Amazon EventBridge rule. To follow that run, use the command in the 
TailLogsCommand
output, which 
cdk deploy
prints when it finishes. A successful run logs 
job_status: COMPLETE
. To start another run outside the schedule, use the command in the 
RunTaskCommand
output after the current run finishes. To list the outputs later, run 
aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name Crawl4aiBedrockKbCrawler --region REGION --query "Stacks[0].Outputs"
.

The deployment guide covers the remaining configuration, including crawl boundaries, the schedule, networking, container architecture, monitoring, and on-demand runs.

Validate retrieval quality

After ingestion, test representative questions with 

Retrieve
before you add generation. A managed knowledge base uses hybrid search. When it uses the default managed embedding model, it also reranks results with its managed reranker. You can narrow results with the metadata from the sidecars. The sample’s default configuration adds 
content_category
set to 
web
to every page. The following example returns up to five chunks from those pages that were crawled in the last seven days. It requires the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) 1.43.32 or later, which you can install with 
python -m pip install "boto3>=1.43.32"
. Replace the Region and knowledge base ID with your own values:

The example passes an integer timestamp, which both knowledge base types accept in number filters. A managed knowledge base doesn’t support the 

startsWith
and 
stringContains
filters. For a customer-managed knowledge base, pass the same filter in 
vectorSearchConfiguration
instead of 
managedSearchConfiguration
. The operators it supports depend on its vector store.

Metadata filtering can improve retrieval precision, but it is not an authorization boundary. If different users should see different pages, the Amazon S3 connector for managed knowledge bases supports document-level access control with access control list (ACL) files that you provide. The sample doesn’t create ACL files.

To generate responses from a managed knowledge base, use agentic retrieval. The 

AgenticRetrieveStream
operation returns the retrieved results and a generated response with citations to those results. For a customer-managed knowledge base, use 
RetrieveAndGenerate
. In both cases, each cited result includes the 
source_url
metadata from its sidecar, which your application can present as the user-facing source.

Evaluate retrieval relevance, source-page coverage, and citation quality whenever you change content preparation, chunking, or retrieval settings. For the retrieval settings that you can tune, see Configure and customize queries for managed knowledge bases.

Running it repeatedly

Each scheduled event launches one standalone Fargate task. The stack doesn’t prevent overlapping runs, so choose an interval longer than the expected crawl and ingestion duration. A failed run isn’t announced, because the sample adds no retry policy, dead-letter queue, or alarm. An ingestion job can also report 

COMPLETE
when some documents fail to ingest, and the task then exits with code 0. The task logs the job’s failure reasons. Add the monitoring you need, including an alarm on those failure reasons, before you rely on the schedule.

Each run incurs Fargate charges for the configured task size, which defaults to 2 vCPU and 4 GB. The task keeps running while it polls the ingestion job for up to 30 minutes, so a slow ingestion job extends billable task time. If ingestion takes longer, the task exits with a nonzero code, and the ingestion job keeps running. The stack turns on Container Insights for the cluster, and flow logs for an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) that it creates. Both add Amazon CloudWatch charges. The stack’s AWS KMS key has a monthly charge, and the task’s public IPv4 address is billed while the task runs. With 

egressMode=nat
or 
privateEndpoints=true
, the NAT gateway and interface endpoints are billed hourly, even when no task is running. Knowledge base usage is billed separately. For details, see Amazon VPC pricing and Amazon Bedrock pricing.

Uploads are additive: removing a URL or missing a page during a later crawl doesn’t delete its existing S3 objects. To remove stale content, delete the obsolete document and matching sidecar under the configured prefix, then start ingestion again. If you turn on the document deletion safeguard (deletion protection) for a managed knowledge base data source, check its threshold. A sync that would delete more than that percentage of documents skips its delete phase, so those documents stay indexed. To start ingestion automatically whenever objects in the bucket change, see Build and deploy an automatic sync solution for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

Responsible AI considerations

Retrieved passages become the context that a foundation model uses to generate a response. Apply the following controls before you run this workflow in production:

  • Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: Attach a guardrail to your agentic retrieval or 
    RetrieveAndGenerate
    requests to apply content filters, denied topics, word filters, and sensitive information filters. Agentic retrieval supports only the guardrail 
    BLOCK
    action, not 
    MASK
    .
  • Contextual grounding checks: Turn on the Guardrails contextual grounding check to score each response for grounding against the retrieved passages and for relevance to the query. The guardrail blocks responses that score below the thresholds you set. For agentic retrieval, you can run the check on the generated answer with the 
    ApplyGuardrail
    API. The check supports question answering and summarization, not conversational chatbot use cases.
  • Treat crawled content as untrusted input: Prepared web pages become model context, so text on a public page can attempt prompt injection through retrieval. Don’t rely on guardrails alone to catch it. Restrict seed URLs to sites you trust, and apply the ingestion filtering patterns described in the next section before content reaches the knowledge base.
  • Citations and human review: Return citations with every generated response so users can verify claims against the source page. For higher-risk use cases, keep a human reviewer in the loop.

Security and compliance considerations

Review the following considerations before you run this workflow against production content:

  • Use trusted public crawl targets: Seed URLs and crawl settings are deployment configuration, and the Fargate task allows outbound access so it can reach public websites. In the sample’s default networking mode, the task runs in a public subnet with a public IP. Configure only authorized public sites. Don’t use this sample to crawl private or internal endpoints. Review network egress and destination controls before adapting the workflow for other trust models.
  • Respect crawl directives: The workflow turns on Crawl4AI’s 
    robots.txt
    check by default, and the CDK path pins it on with no context key to disable it. Verify you have authorization to crawl the target sites, consistent with the AWS Acceptable Use Policy.
  • Rate limiting: Configure delays between requests to avoid overwhelming source websites.
  • Encryption at rest: The stack creates an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key with automatic key rotation and encrypts its CloudWatch log groups with it. Amazon S3 encrypts new objects with server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) by default. If your data classification requires a customer managed key for the bucket, configure the bucket to use it. Then grant the uploader and the knowledge base service role the required AWS KMS permissions in both AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and the key policy. The stack’s task role doesn’t include AWS KMS permissions. A managed knowledge base encrypts its data with an AWS owned key by default, or with a customer managed key that you specify when you create it. For a customer-managed knowledge base, review encryption for its vector store.
  • Least privilege IAM: The CDK stack grants the Fargate task role 
    s3:PutObject
    on the configured bucket prefix. It also grants 
    bedrock:StartIngestionJob
    and 
    bedrock:GetIngestionJob
    on the target knowledge base, plus 
    ssm:GetParameter
    for its single configuration parameter. Separate roles cover Amazon EventBridge task launch and the standard container image pull and log delivery. The pipeline doesn’t read or list S3 and doesn’t call 
    InvokeModel
    or 
    Retrieve
    .
  • Container and template checks: The container runs as a non-root user, and the CDK app runs cdk-nag AWS Solutions checks on every synthesis with resource-scoped suppressions.
  • Protect deployment configuration: The CDK app stores non-secret pipeline settings in a plaintext Parameter Store 
    String
    parameter. Only the parameter name is placed in the task definition. Don’t put passwords, cookies, tokens, or other secrets in CDK context or this parameter.
  • Ingestion pipeline security: See Securing the RAG ingestion pipeline: Filtering mechanisms for filtering and validation patterns to apply before content reaches the knowledge base.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources created during this walkthrough:

  • From the repository’s 
    deploy/
    directory, run 
    cdk destroy
    in the same Region, with the same four required 
    -c
    values that you passed to 
    cdk deploy
    . The app checks them on every command. This removes the stack’s Amazon EventBridge rule, ECS cluster, task definition, log groups, IAM roles, Parameter Store parameter, and security groups, and the VPC if the stack created it. It also schedules the stack’s AWS KMS key for deletion after a 30-day waiting period. It doesn’t delete an imported VPC, your knowledge base, your S3 bucket, or the objects that the workflow uploaded. CDK also keeps the container image and templates in its bootstrap resources. It also leaves the cluster’s Container Insights log group, whose name starts with 
    /aws/ecs/containerinsights/Crawl4aiBedrockKbCrawler-
    .
  • To remove the ingested web content, delete the prepared objects under 
    s3:///
    and sync the data source again. If the document deletion safeguard is on for a managed knowledge base data source, a sync that would delete more than its threshold percentage of documents skips its delete phase.
  • Delete the managed knowledge base only if you created it solely for this walkthrough. A managed knowledge base has no separate vector store to delete.
  • For a customer-managed knowledge base, delete the Amazon S3 data source only if you created it for this walkthrough. Its data deletion policy determines whether Amazon Bedrock also deletes the data source’s vector embeddings from your vector store.

Conclusion

In this post, you learned how to extend Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to authorized public web content that needs preparation before ingestion. A scheduled Fargate task uses Crawl4AI for bounded crawling, prepares Markdown with 

page.md.metadata.json
sidecars, uploads them to an Amazon S3 data source, and starts ingestion. The knowledge base then handles parsing, chunking, embeddings, indexing, retrieval, and grounded responses with citations.

Start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler in a managed knowledge base for most public websites. Use the Crawl4AI path when you need control over which part of each page is indexed or which metadata travels with it. To get started, deploy the scheduled Fargate workflow from the companion sample-crawl4ai-bedrock-knowledge-base repository, and then validate retrieval quality and citations with representative content before scaling.

Learn more

For more information about the services and patterns in this post, refer to the following resources:

Acknowledgments

This product includes software developed by UncleCode as part of the Crawl4AI project.

entries.title: Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI
entries.summary: Agentic assistants built on frontier models run a multi-step tool loop, and paying frontier prices on every step is hard to sustain at production scale. This post shows how to use sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD) to transfer a frontier teacher's agentic behavior into a small, lower-cost student on Amazon SageMaker AI.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI

You built a shopping assistant on a frontier model, and it works. A shopper asks for “a black waist bag under twenty dollars from a shop with at least 4.5 stars,” and the agent searches the catalog, inspects candidates, checks the constraints, and commits to a recommendation. But what does that interaction actually cost? An agentic assistant is not one model call, it is a loop: search, read results, refine, verify, decide. A single completed task can be multiple calls to that frontier model, and you pay for every one, on every shopper. At production scale, that per-task cost compounds, erodes the project’s ROI, and stops the project from shipping.

One way to make an agentic application more efficient is to use a smaller model, which is faster to respond and more cost-effective to host. The catch is quality: a smaller model usually falls short on the task, which is why the larger one was chosen in the first place. Knowledge distillation closes that gap by transferring the behavior of the larger “teacher” model into a smaller “student”, training the student to reproduce the teacher’s outputs, so it keeps much of the quality at the smaller model’s speed and cost.

In this post you will learn how to use knowledge distillation, and specifically sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD), to fine-tune a shopping agent on Amazon SageMaker AI. We cover how to generate high-quality multi-step trajectories with a frontier teacher and keep the ones that solve the task, how to encode them for supervised fine-tuning, how to run the training on serverless infrastructure, and how to evaluate the student against a held-out benchmark.

What is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD)?

The simplest applicable form of distillation is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD). It uses a teacher model to generate high-quality responses, then trains a student model on those responses with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text, with no access to teacher logits and no reinforcement-learning infrastructure, so it works even with a closed or API-only teacher. Compared to other approaches such as logit-based or on-policy, it sits at the most cost-effective and portable end of the distillation spectrum. The teacher writes the answers, and the student is fine-tuned on them. Because those answers persist as a dataset, you can reuse them to train or test different students without regenerating the data.

In principle, you would want the student to match the teacher’s full distribution over possible outputs. The caveat here is that you can’t. The space of possible sequences is astronomically large, so matching it exactly isn’t feasible. SeqKD sidesteps that by approximating it with samples the teacher actually produces.

For an agent, the sequence the teacher produces is not a block of prose but a trajectory, an ordered run of reasoning, tool calls, and the observations they return, where each step is conditioned on everything before it. Training the student on that whole sequence teaches it the reasoning that leads to each action and the multi-step course of action itself, not a single paragraph of answer text. That makes an agentic task one of the cleanest illustrations of sequence-level KD, because the sequence being copied is the behavior itself.

When SeqKD is the right choice

SeqKD fits a specific set of situations:

You have the inputs but no high-quality target outputs

This is the core case for SeqKD, which is fundamentally data generation. You supply the inputs, and the teacher writes the targets, so you can fine-tune on a task or domain that has no existing high-quality labels. The targets can be as simple as single answers or as involved as multi-turn tool-use trajectories. This post takes the demanding end of that spectrum, agentic trajectories, which are especially hard to source. A single task branches into many partially correct runs, and telling a solved run from a failed one takes a reliable grader. A benchmark with a programmatic scorer supplies exactly that, so you can let the teacher generate trajectories and keep only the ones that solve the task.

Your teacher is a frontier model you can only reach through an API

This is the normal case for frontier models. You can’t access the weights to host it yourself, you can’t read its logits, and you can’t fine-tune it. That rules out logit-based distillation and on-policy methods, which all need that internal access. SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text responses, so it is the one approach that still works, and it frees you from paying frontier prices on every request after the student takes over.

You want a strong, cost-effective first step

Some of the strongest small reasoning models were built in significant part with SeqKD (supervised fine-tuning on teacher reasoning traces), so it is an effective starting point for reasoning transfer when the setup is right. The DeepSeek-R1 distilled models are a well-known example: the reasoning of a large teacher was distilled into smaller Qwen and Llama students by fine-tuning them on the teacher’s generated reasoning traces.

Prerequisites

To run this example, you need:

  • An AWS account with an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role for SageMaker AI that has read and write access to an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket and permission to invoke your teacher model.
  • A frontier teacher model to generate the trajectories (this walkthrough uses one on Amazon Bedrock).
  • Access to SageMaker AI model customization in a supported AWS Region.
  • Amazon SageMaker Studio (or a local IDE with the AWS CLI configured), running a Python 3.12 or higher kernel, with the SageMaker Python SDK v3 and 
    boto3
    (pin your versions). Use an ml.m5.4xlarge instance at minimum for the notebook environment, since the data preparation and local scoring steps run on its CPU.
  • Working knowledge of Python, supervised fine-tuning, and tool-using agents.
  • The accompanying code repository and a task with a programmatic scorer (this walkthrough uses the ShoppingBench test set. Substitute your own task and grader).

Solution overview

This section walks the pipeline from end to end. A frontier teacher, GLM-5.3 on Amazon Bedrock, acts as the ShoppingBench agent to generate trajectories. The benchmark’s own scorer keeps only the ones that solve the task, and those solved trajectories fine-tune a Qwen3.5-4B student with serverless supervised fine-tuning on SageMaker AI model customization. The distilled student is then evaluated on a held-out ShoppingBench split and served behind a SageMaker AI Inference real-time endpoint that runs the tool loop.

Preparing the dataset

Sourcing trajectories worth imitating is the hard part, and the ShoppingBench scorer is what separates the successful runs from the failed ones. ShoppingBench publishes 750 synthesized shopping problems, 250 each for the product, shop, and voucher intents, each with a hidden gold answer and the constraints that define success. We split them once into 426 training problems and 324 held-out evaluation problems (product 103, shop 105, voucher 116), as fixed indices so the two sets don’t overlap.

For each training problem, a frontier teacher, GLM-5.3 on Amazon Bedrock with reasoning on and temperature 1.0, acts as the ShoppingBench agent. It searches the catalog of about 2.7 million products, inspects candidates, and recommends the ones that meet the constraints. We sample the teacher twice per problem, which gives 850 trajectories, then let ShoppingBench’s own scorer keep only the ones that solve the task. Temperature 1.0 is deliberate. Sampling rather than greedy decoding makes the two attempts explore different queries and reasoning paths, which gives more problems at least one solved trajectory and a more diverse set to learn from. This rejection-sampling step turns a capable-but-imperfect teacher into a clean training set, since the teacher only has to be right often enough that the solved runs are worth imitating.

Each solved trajectory is a complete episode: the shopper request, the teacher’s reasoning and tool calls at each step (search, inspect, recommend, terminate), and the observation the environment returned. We keep the reasoning alongside the actions, which the Results show is what carries the student most of the way to its teacher.

Encoding trajectories for training

Sequence-level distillation is supervised learning over trajectories that already exist, so nothing calls a tool during training, and the application only ever sees text. Because these trajectories are multi-step tool-use conversations, we encode each as a 

messages
list of chat turns and let the student’s own chat template render it, so the tokens the trainer sees match the tokens the agent produces at inference.

Each trajectory becomes one training row per step. The 

user
turn carries the system prompt and the conversation so far. The 
assistant
turn carries that step’s reasoning and the tool call it leads to, a … block followed by a [{…}] in the harness’s native form. Loss falls on the 
assistant
turn only, so the model learns to produce the next reasoning-and-action, not to predict the observations the environment returned. A trajectory with several steps expands into several rows. Here the solved trajectories expand to about 2,600 training and 130 validation rows after filtering.

A single row pairs the conversation so far (user) with the one next step to learn (assistant):

Each later step becomes its own row, with the new observation appended to the user content and the next reasoning-and-tool-call as the 

assistant
target, through to the final 
recommend_product
and 
terminate
calls. Render every row with your model’s exact chat template.

Split the data by problem, not by row. The teacher is sampled twice per problem, and each trajectory expands into several steps, so many rows share one problem, and a row-level split would leak near-identical context across training and validation. Holding out whole problems (about five percent) keeps the validation set honest.

The cost of per-step encoding is repeated context, because each row restates the growing conversation, and serverless fine-tuning truncates anything past 

dataset_max_len
, so a row that crosses the limit loses part of what it needs. Rather than let the limit decide what gets cut, keep rows within budget. The most effective fix is to compress tool observations, which dominate the token count. For product search results, keep only the fields the next decision depends on (id, price, rating, and the constraints being checked), drop the raw listing text, and cap how many results you retain per search. If trajectories are still over budget, cap the steps per trajectory. Here 
dataset_max_len
is 16,384 tokens, which fits most trajectories after observations are trimmed.

After the JSONL for each split is in S3, register each as a customization dataset asset with 

DataSet.create
from the SageMaker Python SDK v3, which returns the 
train_dataset
and 
val_dataset
the training job consumes.

Fine-tuning the student

Training uses SageMaker AI model customization with serverless SFT. You select a base model from the model hub, point the job at the encoded datasets, and the managed service provisions the compute, runs the job, and returns the customized model, with metrics tracked in Amazon SageMaker with MLflow. Because the data is already in a supported format, there is no training script, container image, or instance to manage.

The job writes its output into a model package group that versions every model it produces, so create the group first with 

ModelPackageGroup.create
(reusing it if the name already exists) and pass it to the trainer. Then configure the customization job. Choose the base model and training type, point it at the train and validation datasets plus the model package group, then name an MLflow experiment so metrics stream to MLflow while the job runs.

The trainer starts from a documented set of default hyperparameters that you can inspect with 

sft_trainer.hyperparameters.to_dict()
and override before launching. For this run we raise the sequence length to fit the multi-step trajectories, use a Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) rank of 64, and train for three epochs over the small dataset:

Validate the configuration with a dry run, then launch the managed job and read the registered Model Package ARN when it finishes. That ARN is the deploy-ready artifact the evaluation and serving steps consume:

Evaluating the student

Evaluate in two stages, lowest cost first. The full end-to-end evaluation is both time and resource intensive. It stands up a search server over millions of products, deploys the endpoint, and runs a multi-step agent loop on every held-out problem. Before running the full evaluation, run a low-cost managed pre-check using SageMaker AI model evaluation, which scores one generated step at a time against the teacher’s ground-truth action.

The pre-check needs a scoring function. Model evaluation supports a Custom Scorer reward function you supply that runs once per sample, comparing the student’s generated action against the teacher’s. For tool-call distillation, grade tool selection (did the model call the right tools, in order, ignoring argument formatting), because that is the behavior distillation most needs to transfer. To keep the focus on selection rather than syntax, the reward function reads the tool names out of both the student’s action and the teacher’s reference without requiring an exact format match.

Register that function as a versioned 

Evaluator
with 
Evaluator.create()
, then call 
evaluate()
to run one Custom Scorer job per task, scoring the base model alongside the student so every result has a comparison.

The decision rule is straightforward. The student must beat the base model on this low-cost pre-check. If it does, the distillation took and it is worth running the more comprehensive end-to-end evaluation. If it does not, fix training first.

Serving the distilled agent

The distilled model doesn’t run tools on its own. Fine-tuning teaches it to emit the right tool call at the right moment as text, but something still has to execute that call and feed back the result. At inference you wrap the model in a small deterministic harness that prompts the model, parses the tool call it emits, runs the tool, appends the observation, and prompts again, looping until the model produces a final answer. This is ordinary application code, or an off-the-shelf serving framework, not reinforcement learning and not an on-policy training loop.

The student is a Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter over an open-weight base, which shapes how you deploy it. Rather than merge the adapter and serve a second full copy of the weights, serve the base model once and attach the student as an adapter on top, as two inference components on one real-time endpoint. Naming the inference component at invoke time selects which one answers, so the same endpoint serves both the base and the distilled student for a side-by-side comparison.

We serve the open-weight model with the Deep Java Library Large Model Inference (DJL LMI) container, which bundles the vLLM engine for high-throughput generation, pinned to a specific version rather than 

latest
, so redeploys are reproducible. The accompanying notebook wraps the inference-component calls in a small 
kd_serve
helper, so deploying the base component with LoRA serving enabled and then attaching the student adapter reduces to:

The 

instance_types
list is an ordered preference. SageMaker AI Inference deploys on the first type with available capacity and falls back down the list, so the student serves on an 
ml.g5.2xlarge
, 
ml.g6.2xlarge
, or 
ml.g6e.2xlarge
depending on availability. The base weights load once, and both inference components share them, so adding the adapter costs adapter-sized memory instead of a second copy of the model.

Results

We evaluate the distilled student on the held-out ShoppingBench test split, against a set of reference points that bracket what good looks like:

  • Base Qwen3.5-4B: the off-the-shelf student with no fine-tuning. This is the floor.
  • Distilled student (SeqKD): the same 4B model fine-tuned on the teacher trajectories, the approach this post describes. This is the result that matters.
  • GLM-5.3 teacher: the frontier model that generated the training data, on Bedrock. We report it both sampled (temperature 1.0, the setting that produced the data) and greedy (temperature 0).
  • Medium-sized frontier model: a strong proprietary model run as an agent, included as a practical ceiling.

Every model runs the same unmodified ShoppingBench agent loop over the three shopper intents (product, shop, and voucher). We report Absolute Success Rate (ASR), the share of held-out problems the agent solves, averaged over the three intents, with missing trajectories counted as failures. A problem counts as solved when the recommended product or products meet every stated constraint. The following numbers come from a single run with a LoRA student, so expect a few points of run-to-run variation.

Task success

The headline result is the Absolute Success Rate on the 324 held-out problems, broken down by intent and averaged across the three:

ModelproductshopvoucherAverage
Base Qwen3.5-4B (no fine-tuning)0.4560.3140.1210.297
Distilled student (SeqKD)0.5630.6380.4220.541
GLM-5.3 teacher (sampled, temperature 1.0)0.5530.6190.3620.511
GLM-5.3 teacher (greedy, temperature 0)0.5440.6380.4390.540
Medium-sized frontier model0.5830.6670.3880.546

In summary, a 4B model recovered essentially all of its frontier teacher’s task quality, matching it within run-to-run noise. We report the teacher two ways because they answer different questions. Greedy decoding returns the single most likely trajectory, the stronger choice when each model gets one attempt per problem (as in this evaluation) which is why the greedy teacher scores 0.540 against the sampled teacher’s 0.511. We generated the training data the other way, sampling at temperature 1.0 so repeated attempts explored different paths, and the scorer could keep the ones that solved the task. That filtering is also why the student can edge out the sampled teacher it learned from, since rejection sampling trains it only on the teacher’s solved runs, not its average output, so it imitates a best-of slice rather than the full spread of attempts.

Reasoning in the targets matters

The student learns from the teacher’s reasoning as well as its tool calls, and that choice is responsible for a large part of the result. Training the same student on the same trajectories with the reasoning stripped, leaving only the bare tool calls, drops average ASR from 0.541 to 0.415:

Both students clear the base model, so even the tool-calls-only version is a real improvement, but keeping the reasoning is what carries the student the rest of the way to its teacher. The reasoning between the actions isn’t narration to discard, it is part of the behavior that solves the task.

Keeping general ability

ASR measures the skill we distilled for. The counterweight is whether the student kept its general instruction-following ability or overfit to the shopping task. We check with IFEval, a general instruction-following benchmark that scores verifiable format instructions such as “answer in exactly three bullet points.” Treat it as a regression check, not a leaderboard. The student’s prompt-strict score falls from 0.819 for the base model to 0.741, and its instruction-strict score from 0.872 to 0.813, a drop of roughly 6 to 8 points (Figure 6). That is the expected cost of specialization. The student traded some general instruction-following for a large gain on the shopping task. A much larger drop would be the warning sign that distillation narrowed the model too far.

Benefits and tradeoffs

A success rate on its own doesn’t justify the switch. The reason to distill is that you get most of the stronger model’s quality at the small model’s cost and speed. The clearest evidence here is that the 4B student reaches the task quality of its frontier teacher and a medium-sized frontier model, while being small enough to serve on a single G family instance (NVIDIA A10G/L40/L40S in this example).

The cost difference is as much about shape as size. A frontier model reached through an API is billed per token, on every step of every task, so the cost grows with usage and doesn’t stop, and the agentic loop from the introduction pays that toll every time. The distilled student runs on an endpoint you host, which bills for the instance by the hour whether it serves one task or thousands, so added traffic costs nothing more until you scale out. You’re trading a variable per-request charge for a fixed hourly one, and the smaller the model you can get away with, the smaller that fixed cost is.

We don’t publish a per-task cost or latency number here because it depends on your traffic: the throughput a G family instance sustains, and therefore the cost amortized per task, is a function of your request pattern, sequence lengths, and concurrency. Measure it on your own workload against the current SageMaker AI pricing and your frontier provider’s token pricing, rather than relying on a single headline figure.

Limitations and best practices

Will the task fit the student (the capacity wall)

Distillation transfers a distribution the student can already represent, not raw capability it lacks. Across too large a gap, the student copies the teacher’s format without learning to solve. A small model trained on a large teacher’s chains of thought produces long, well-structured reasoning whose answers stay wrong, and an agent trained the same way emits well-formed tool calls that make no progress, re-searches with reworded queries, and runs to its step limit without meeting the constraints. The symptom is the same in both, traces lengthen while accuracy stays flat. When you see it, stop adding data and either grow the student or lower task difficulty.

The gap that decides this is between the task and the student, not between the student and the teacher. A small student can recover a much larger teacher’s quality as long as the task itself is within its reach. That is why the shopping agent here works. The teacher is a mixture-of-experts model with roughly 40 billion active parameters, about ten times the student’s 4 billion, but the shopping task is well within a 4B model’s capacity, so the student recovers the teacher’s quality instead of only lengthening its trajectories.

Where SeqKD stops helping

SeqKD lifts easy and mid-difficulty problems but plateaus on the hardest ones, where the student must recover from its own mistakes. This is sharper for an agent than a single-step task. In a multi-step loop an early error compounds, because the student doesn’t see the states its own mistakes lead to. Closing that gap is what on-policy methods target, which is why SeqKD is usually the first stage rather than the finish line. SeqKD also asks the least of your infrastructure, since it uses only the teacher’s text, whereas logit distillation needs the teacher’s per-token distribution and on-policy methods score the student’s own rollouts. A text-only SeqKD warm start followed by an on-policy stage is a common recipe, so this post covers the first stage and pushing past the plateau is the natural next step.

Two choices that carry the result

First, match the training targets to the behavior you want. Here that meant keeping the teacher’s reasoning with each tool call rather than compressing to final answers, since the reasoning is part of what solves the task (the Results quantify the gap), and rendering every target with the chat template the agent uses at serving time. Second, evaluate honestly. Measure on data the models have not seen, since leaked benchmarks inflate scores, and compare against more than the untrained base model the student is bound to beat, setting it beside the teacher and an independent frontier model so the number shows how close the student came to what it was distilled from.

Cleaning up

A real-time inference endpoint bills for as long as it runs, so tear down the endpoint that you stood up for serving after you have your results. Because the student is served as an adapter inference component on top of a base inference component, the pieces must come down in dependency order: the adapter component first, then the base component, then the endpoint and its configuration. The accompanying 

kd_serve
helper does this for you, finding the adapter structurally so it cleans up regardless of the exact component names:

The training job itself needs no cleanup. Serverless training provisions compute, runs, and releases it automatically, so a completed job isn’t an ongoing charge. The registered model package and its group carry no compute cost either, so you can keep them for lineage and redeploy later. The one thing that does keep costing you is your data in S3 (the encoded trajectories and output artifacts), which incurs storage cost for as long as you keep it, so delete what you no longer need or move it to a lower-cost storage class.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to distill an agentic shopping assistant into a smaller, lower-cost student with sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD). We generated high-quality single-turn, multi-step trajectories with a frontier teacher on Bedrock and kept only the ones that solved the task using ShoppingBench’s own scorer, encoded each step as chat-formatted messages that preserve the teacher’s reasoning alongside its tool calls, fine-tuned the student on serverless infrastructure with SageMaker AI model customization, tracked training with MLflow, ran a quality gate check with SageMaker AI model evaluation, and served the result behind an inference endpoint that runs the tool loop. The payoff was a 4B student that recovers essentially all of its frontier teacher’s task quality. Because SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text outputs, it works even when the teacher is a closed frontier model you reach through an API, and you can stop paying frontier prices on every step after the student takes over.

SeqKD is a strong first step with real limits. Match the student size to the task, evaluate on a held-out suite against strong reference points rather than only the untrained base model, and when the hardest tail of problems resists imitation, follow SeqKD with on-policy methods not covered here that let the student learn from its own rollouts.

To try this yourself, see the accompanying code repository and the SageMaker AI documentation.

entries.title: Agentic engineering intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
entries.summary: Learn how to build a multi-agent engineering assistant that compresses aerospace component substitution evaluation from days to minutes, using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the Strands Agents SDK to assemble substitution evidence while keeping the engineer as the decision-maker.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Agentic engineering intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

When a qualified aerospace component goes obsolete or hits a long lead time, an engineer spends days cross-referencing specifications across vendor datasheets, interface control documents (ICDs), and qualification records before documenting a substitution justification for review. An incorrect substitution on a flight-critical component can cause mission failure, yet the evidence trail behind each decision is often spread across email and undocumented institutional knowledge, so there is no formal, repeatable package for a reviewer to check.

A previous post, Manufacturing intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, showed how the model retrieves answers locked inside engineering diagrams, thermal plots, and datasheet charts that text-only pipelines miss. This post picks up where that retrieval work left off, putting those capabilities inside a multi-agent system that assembles substitution evidence, from retrieval to a drafted assessment.

In this post, we show how to build a multi-agent engineering assistant that cuts the manual cross-referencing behind part substitution evaluation using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, and the open source Strands Agents SDK. A planner routes work across three specialist agents that search a multimodal knowledge base, score candidates against deterministic tolerance rules, compare part photos, and ground lifecycle claims in live web data. The engineer remains the decision-maker throughout, because the system assembles evidence and drafts documents without ever approving a substitution on its own.

Solution overview

The assistant is built around one design rule, which is that the engineer makes every decision and the system assembles the evidence for it. That rule determines where we use large language models (LLMs) and where we use deterministic code instead.

Three pillars define the architecture:

  • Deterministic spec-fit evaluation – Tolerance-rule code written in Python scores each candidate part against the reference part and the engineer’s stated requirements. Because the same inputs consistently produce the same pass/flag verdicts, the results can go into a formal engineering review.
  • Multi-agent orchestration – A lightweight planner routes each query to one or more of three specialist agents (Catalog, Evaluation, Knowledge), and a supervisor synthesizes their findings only when more than one specialist contributed. Complex questions such as “Check if this wheel is going end-of-life, find alternatives, and score them” chain all three specialists in sequence.
  • Human-in-the-loop decision – The system drafts justification memos and Integration Impact Assessments for engineering review, but it doesn’t recommend or approve a substitution. Every evaluation also writes an audit trail entry aligned with AS9100 sections 8.4 and 8.5.6.

The following diagram shows the architecture.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. In this solution, chat requests from the engineer’s application flow into a multi-agent graph hosted on AgentCore runtime: a planner (Claude Haiku 5.5) produces a routing plan, specialists (Claude Sonnet 5.5) execute their tools, and a supervisor (Claude Opus 5.5) synthesizes their results when more than one specialist ran. The specialists retrieve from a managed knowledge base that we created with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, routed through an AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, alongside the Web Search connector for live web data. For image-as-query (uploading a chart to identify a part), the agent calls a native Amazon S3 Vectors index directly, because the managed knowledge base retrieval API doesn’t accept image input. Amazon S3 Vectors is a capability of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). A separate fixed chain (Knowledge, then Evaluation, then Supervisor) produces the formal Integration Impact Assessment (IIA) document.

Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings appears in two distinct roles:

  • Multimodal retrieval – Datasheets, ICDs, and performance charts are embedded with Nova Multimodal Embeddings so text and visual content share one semantic space. An engineer can enter “torque curve for the 0.06 Nms wheel” or upload a chart image, and retrieval returns the matching diagram with source attribution.
  • Visual similarity scoring – When two candidate parts are compared, Nova Multimodal Embeddings produces a quantitative cosine similarity between their photos, and Claude analyzes the specific physical differences (mounting pattern, connector placement, housing geometry). The score adds supporting evidence to the deterministic spec comparison, which is what the fit verdict is based on.

Prerequisites

To follow along, you need:

  • An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region.
  • Model access to Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Opus 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock. For model availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
  • A managed knowledge base created with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases, using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings over your parts corpus (datasheets, ICDs, descriptions) for text and document retrieval.
  • An Amazon S3 Vectors index over your part photos and datasheet chart crops, for the image-as-query path.
  • An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with the Web Search connector and a managed knowledge base target.
  • Python 3.10 or later and Jupyter for running the notebooks.
  • Docker, if you adapt the deployment recipe in notebook 03 to host the agent on AgentCore runtime.
  • The sample code from the GitHub repository.

Solution walkthrough

The following sections describe each part of the system in the order a query uses it. We start with the parts corpus and the specialist agents, then cover routing, deterministic scoring, the two ways the assistant uses Nova Multimodal Embeddings, the fixed chain that produces formal documents, and deployment to AgentCore runtime.

The complete code sample is a set of five Jupyter notebooks in the GitHub repository, and each notebook runs on its own. The notebooks import from 

mei_core
, a self-contained copy of the agent and tool modules in the same folder, and they include their own parts data, chart crops, and evaluation query set. You can run every snippet in this post from the notebooks without other application code.

Structure the parts corpus

The sample dataset is seven reaction wheels from a fictional manufacturer (AnyCompany) spanning 0.003–5.0 Nms of momentum storage. Each part is a folder that pairs structured data with the source documents an engineer actually reads, and this mix is what makes the corpus multimodal. The 

specs.json
file holds the machine-readable fields that drive deterministic scoring, while the ICD, product photo, and rendered datasheet page carry the visual and narrative detail that structured fields leave out.

The 

specs.json
file captures both the engineering specifications and a lifecycle profile, which is what lets the assistant flag obsolescence and lead-time risk alongside spec fit.

The 

vendor
field is stated explicitly for every part. Because catalog folder IDs and file names are reused across datasets, every specialist prompt treats the structured 
vendor
value returned by 
get_part_specs
as authoritative and is forbidden from guessing a manufacturer from an ID, a file name, a photo, or a web search result. Taking the manufacturer from structured data keeps the assistant from attributing a part to the wrong supplier because the model thinks it recognizes the hardware.

Each part folder also carries two assets that text-only indexing cannot use. The product photo feeds visual similarity scoring, and the rendered datasheet page carries torque-box and torque-curve plots that answer performance questions no OCR text layer captures. Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings embeds both into the same vector space as the text, so a query can match a spec value, a paragraph, or a plot.

The following sample shows four datasheet pages from the corpus, spanning three orders of magnitude of momentum storage.

The template repeats across the family, but the product photo and the pair of performance plots change with every part. These Regions show the housing geometry, mounting pattern, torque envelope, and power draw, which the spec fields don’t state directly, so we embed them alongside the text.

Define specialists with scoped tools

Each specialist is a Strands agent with a narrow prompt and only the tools it needs. Scoping tools per specialist keeps behavior predictable, because the Knowledge specialist has no access to the catalog discovery tools and the Catalog specialist has no access to the evaluation tools. The following code creates the Evaluation specialist.

The following diagram shows how the planner routes a query to the specialists and when the supervisor synthesizes their results. The list after it describes what each specialist does.

  • Catalog – Discovers parts through knowledge base search and exhaustive spec filtering (
    kb_search
    , 
    filter_parts_by_spec
    , 
    get_part_specs
    , 
    get_substitution_requirements
    ).
  • Evaluation – Scores candidates deterministically and compares parts visually (
    score_substitution_fit
    , 
    compare_parts
    , 
    visual_similarity_score
    , 
    check_qualification_status
    , 
    generate_substitution_memo
    ).
  • Knowledge – Answers questions from datasheets and ICDs, checks live end-of-life status, and retrieves visual content (
    get_part_specs
    , 
    web_search_eol
    , 
    retrieve_visual_content
    ).

Use a small model for routing and a large model for synthesis

Routing is a classification task with no tool calls, so it doesn’t need a large reasoning model. A Haiku-based planner returns a numbered routing plan in a couple of seconds. The Opus supervisor runs only when two or more specialists contributed, because synthesizing a single specialist’s already-complete answer adds about 8 seconds of latency with no quality gain.

Splitting the work across three model tiers matches cost and latency to each stage. Haiku classifies the query, Sonnet runs the tools, and Opus writes the combined answer, which is the step where response quality matters most.

Keep the scoring deterministic

The spec-fit evaluation runs as ordinary Python code against a hand-written requirements schema. The schema defines the critical specs and tolerance rules for each component category, and 

score_substitution_fit
compares each spec, counts passes and flags, and surfaces lifecycle risk. Because the verdict must be reproducible for an engineering review package, no LLM is involved in this step.

The tool returns a structured verdict with an explicit disclaimer:
